blocks.x: What's that? Waiters don't get nothing? No.
Can we get your name? Can we get your name? What's your right name? My name is Edward B. Garland.
What's the B for? Bertrand. Oh, you kind of a lot of Bertrands?
I guess so.
Buddy Bertrand? And what's your name, the man with the camera over there?

My name is Floyd Levin, but I'm going to tell you something, Tutti, all these years I never knew. My middle name is Bertrand. Would you believe that? I don't know about that. Bertrand, yes, I've kept that a secret. Well, it's, uh...
Uh, well, you got another name too that everybody calls you that you love so... You must love that, huh?
M-O-N-T-U-D-I-E.
What does that mean in English, or should I ask?
I'm the Duke.
The Duke, huh?
I see.
Where'd you get that name? Well, I got that name...
This old guy around New York they used to call... Montutti. Oh, yeah. And, uh...
The boys all used to...

Holler at each other, you know. He might do something. Johnny Dotslider would come in a little late or something, and... They'd come on there, you look like old Montutti. What band was that? Kid Horry. Kid Horry, huh? In New York? When was he in New York with Johnny Dots? Johnny Dots was in New York with us. When was that? What year was that? That was... I was, uh...
Seven o'clock.
Let's see how it... Was that before the war or after World War I?
That was, uh... Before the war or after World War I?
That was, uh... Four o'clock. Yeah. I was...
I was, uh... I was, uh... Three o'clock.
When was that? What year was that? Seven o'clock.
Let's see. I left. Was that before the war or after World War I? That was, uh... Before. Before World War I. Yeah. Were you here when they had the big storm? Let me see, I left.
Was that before the war or after World War I?
It was before.
Before World War I?
Yeah.
Were you here when they had the big storm?
Here in the island?
Mm-hmm, when they had the big storm. Do you remember that big storm in September 1915?
No, I wasn't here. You weren't here? 1915? Oh, no. I left here in 1912.
Well, where did you go when you left?
Went straight from here to Chicago.
And then where did you go?
I went to play with Mabel E. Lane in a New Orleans jazz band.

Oh, you know, Louis Kepert was playing on it. I had Louis Kepert with me. Just recently, Louis Kepert got hit by a police car. Oh, yeah? Yeah, it could only happen to Louis Kepert. Oh, my goodness. You know, get hit by a police car. Oh. Is this seriously her? No, no, I think he can walk around and talk. He can still talk, I'll tell you that.
Well, I've taken him from here.
Yeah.
Louis Kepert, Johnny, Johnny, uh, Sugar Johnny on trumpet. I had a rip home on trombone, Lions Dewey on clarinet, and, uh, Herbert Lindsay on violin.
Mm-hmm.
And I was on bass.
Mm-hmm.

And when it was a take happy, and just before the train pulled out, a telegram, and come up, and the man was looking out for the band. He sent them off. Come up and stuff. Happy, happy. Had the drums fixing to get up on the train with him. Oh, yeah. Yeah. That's red happy. Yeah. Red happy boat. A little happy crowd.
What happened, uh, did you have to use a Yankee drummer?
No.
Isn't that one of those damn bands?
We didn't use no drum at all. Oh, no. We cut the drum out.
That's... Well, how did you get to New York? I never did get that part of the story straight.

We went there, we went there on, uh, we went there to play, uh, uh, I think we played, uh, I don't know, played on the show or something. Or a theater. Oh, you toured, huh? Yeah, and then we played in this club, you know, a couple of nights, you know. We got a... give us a little gig in this...
Yeah, where was the club? Oh, well, don't work, don't strain your brain. Save it for something important.
Yeah, save it for something important.
And I just wondered, because I didn't know much about jazz in New York in those early days, and, you know, New Orleans music, anyway, I'll call it.
Well, at that time, they said the only jazz band.
Yeah. But they used to say something else before that. Mm-hmm. Didn't they? Yeah. What did they say? What words did they have for the music when you were coming up?
Ragtime.
Ragtime?
Mm-hmm.
Well, before my time, they used to call it ratty music. Did you ever hear that?
Yeah. A lot of people wouldn't hire us. They'd say they want that ratty band.
That's right. Was the original Dixieland jazz band in New York when you were there, do you think? No. Because they were there just before the Lord. You knew that guy they called?
Oh, you knew the Red? Red Nichols, you mean? No, no.
No. No. What was his name? Monkey?
Used to be the drummer?
That's the drummer. Yeah. What did you call him? You called him Monkey, huh? Spargo. Spargo.
Spargo. Yeah.
Tony. Mm-hmm. Did you know Harry Shields and Eddie Edwards and all those? Sure.
Nick LaRocco? I knew all them guys.
Oh, yeah? Did they follow you around when they were youngsters?
In the Orleans, yeah. You know, I can't think I'm in the Orleans.
You can't believe me.

I can't believe them in the Orleans. Yeah, it's true. These fellas all around. We'd be out in Irish Channel playing those dances, you know? Lawn parties? Lawn parties, they call them. I understand why across the lot and torch lights, you know? Hanging a string of torch lights, you know?
Did you know Kid Punch? Yeah. I talked to him this morning. He's been sick, but they let him out. He's been in the hospital? Yeah, he's out now. He's home. I'll give you his phone number.
Is that right?
Yeah. I just put a little article in the newspaper, you know, because he wants to hear from all of his friends while they're here.
Oh.
So, he's got his newspaper, a number coming out in the newspaper. But that Irish Channel was a nice quiet place, wasn't it?
No, I lived out in Irish Channel for a while.
Oh, right.
Where? 743 Felicity Street.
You mean Felicity. That's correct.
That is correct. They call it Felicity. Felicity Road. Yeah. Yeah. Well, we didn't say Felicity, we said Felicity.
Yeah.
Melpamine. Melpamine. Yeah. Melpamine. Yeah. Melpamine.
Did you say Socrates? Huh? Did you ever go across the river to Socrates Street or Copernicus? You never did go across the river much? Yeah.
You know those three?
Now, what part?
Algiers or Gretna? Algiers.
That's where they have Socrates.
I mean, Algiers.
I used to live over there. That's when I was taking lessons from Thess, Moneta. Moneta. Yeah, I used to take lessons from him. Manuel?
Manuel Moneta? Oh, horse. Horse?
Why'd you call him that?
Hmm?
Why'd you call him horse?
Because we always did call him horse. All around the district. He was playing down the district. Horse.
Did he stomp his feet much then? When you put him in a stall? No.
Nobody was stomping his feet. If this was a name they had for him, horse. Well, you know, he used to be nervous like that.
Yeah. Maybe he was worried about another mule or something.
He was playing piano down in the district. You know what I mean.
Yeah, I know. If I thought it was going to be that kind of interview, I wouldn't have stayed around.
Okay. No, I won't talk.
I got a bad mouth. I got a fever blusht out of my mouth. You see, so I got a bad mouth. Now, what about your brother Johnny? Johnny Garland.

Who did he play with? Johnny didn't play with any particular person. When he was here. Because he said he never let music interfere with a job. He tried to teach me that. Always keep a job. It would depend on music. I couldn't see it that way. Oh, music. He was a blueprint. Which kind of? Blueprint. Oh, yeah. Like Louie Warnick.
Louie Warnick.
A saxophone player?
Yeah, yeah. He was a blueprint man too. My brother's one.
For Dietzchen, I think. Is he living yet, Louie?
No, no. He's been there. No, I didn't. For Dietzchen, I think.
Is he living yet, Louie?
No, no, he's been there.
No, I didn't. He stayed around here in Wack. He used to play. Different people.
Short bands? Short bands.
And he played a while with all of them.
Oh, your brother? Yeah.
His mother. Yeah. And, uh, it goes after that, we got another Johnny. Johnny, uh, Brown.
Johnny Brown? I thought he was a bass player. That Johnny Brown.
Johnny Brown played violin.
I must be thinking about Jimmy Brown. Jimmy Brown played with the Imperial.
Yeah.
I get them all confused.
Johnny Brown. Yeah. I mean, Octo.
Who was Johnny Brown? I can't place that name at all.
He played the violin.
Oh, he's the one who took up clarinet.
He was playing clarinet, yeah.
Yeah, and Chris Kelly stole his band from him. I know who you're talking about now. Yeah.
Yeah. Uh, they, uh,

had, uh, Johnny Brown was playing. Johnny Dodge used to work for Johnny Brown. Mm-hmm. Johnny Brown had a furniture wagon, you know? Mm-hmm. Then Johnny Brown used to be around those auctions, you know, around those prawn lids, you know? Mm-hmm. All in there. Yeah. And, uh, they used to haul them. Different items, you know, that people buy furniture and stuff, you know? And things like that. Then they'd get to deliver them. Johnny used to work on the, work for him.
And one day I come along,
Johnny was sitting on like a tailgate. Mm-hmm.
Mm-hmm.
And he was blowing his clarinet. You know, he stopped there. I stood up first and listened, you know. He was just running over some things, you know?
So I walked up there, uh,

the... How would you like to play in the band? Who are you playing with? I ain't playing with nobody. You know, they come from over, Bay St. Louis. So I ain't playing with nobody. How would you like to play with a... Kid Horry. I wanna call him Horry's band. I said, all right. I said, will you come to rehearsal? He said, yeah. So I told him... That I'd see Horry, and I'd seen Horry and told him Horry. I said, I think he'll be all right, Horry. So... Well, he said, have him come on over. We have rehearsal. We have rehearsal. We have rehearsal. He come on over there. Johnny come on over there and... Fitted in all right with us. Start the playin'. We should fight every night.
This is Johnny which? Johnny Dodge.
Oh, Johnny Dodge. Fight every night.
Y'all must have been real good friends.
We were. As soon as we get through, we go somewhere... We leave, we go on around, and touch the restaurant, eat, then go down by the Eagle Saloon. Drink. Fight didn't last long.
Well, who would carry the lead in those times?
Who carried the lead?
Yeah.
The violin player.
Oh, yeah.
And the big guy played violin first. He was a good one.
You know his nephew is here, Alec.
Alec, yeah, the drummer? That's Bonnie's brother, Alec.
That's Bonnie, the drummer.
Yeah, Bonnie's brother.
And he's still going. Yeah.
Yeah.
He laid off for a while, but he's coming back, you know. You can't quit. Well, I don't understand how a band worked when you had the violin lead. Then what did the clarinet play?
You couldn't understand what the...
Well, what the clarinet would play if the violin played the lead, huh? Would he play lead, too, or would he play variations, or what?
Well, when the violin would play, he'd play the melody, or the clarinet, playing the harmony. Mm-hmm. We'd run crazy, we'd run all around, you know. Yeah.
Well, now what about the trumpet then, the clarinet, rather?
The trumpet, the trombone, work together.
They'd work together, then.
Yeah. The trumpet, play the melody, the trombone, play... I'd play, uh... I'd play the harbacarbet to him.

Yeah, I see, yeah. Did that... How did that work? Or did it sound at all when they were playing by head? When they were playing that way? Did it sound at all like the Red Book then? You remember the Red Book? Yeah. Yeah, did it sound like the Red Book at all? Yeah. What was the difference between a reading band and a non-reading band, you know, a head band? What was the difference? What made the difference, then?

What made the difference, you know, take a band that's playing them notes, playing my notes, they played... They had the arrangement, they had the arrangement for different instruments. Mm-hmm. You understand? Mm-hmm. One played the third, the second, the fourth, you understand? Mm-hmm. And on. I know.
We've got Robichaux's library, we've got 7,000 orchestrations of his. Yeah, we have?
Yeah, up at Tulane where I work.
Yeah? You ought to see them.
You got John's, huh? Yeah. I don't remember that band.
I don't know...
They're still using those things, they're still using Red Book. I don't know that band. When we first had that band, they had Henry Kimmel on the bass.
Mm-hmm.

He had Charlie McCurtis on the clarinet. Mm-hmm. He had Buddy Christian on the guitar. Walter Brundee on the drums. Mm-hmm. And John was on the violin. And Kimmel, not Andrew Kimmel, before Andrew Kimmel was a fellow that built. Jim Williams was playing trumpet. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. That's before Andrew, and Kimball came in.
Yeah, and Kimball was with him in the 20s, I believe. Late years.
Yeah, that was the band.

Yeah, I'm sure of that, because Alvin Alcorn told me that Kimball would play some of the Jolly Roll Morton numbers that got published, you know, from the orchestration, and he could really get hot. Which I never knew that Kimball was a hot man at all, I didn't know he was a get-off man.
Oh, Andrew?
Yeah.
Well, he wasn't too hot, he was pretty good.
Was he hotter than Manuel Perez?

I'm going to tell you that there you are, there's two good men, two good men you call in there, Manuel and Kimball. Both. I don't know, I don't know, there wasn't a mood. There wasn't too hot on the jazz, you know. They played, there was good trumpet players.
Good musician, good trumpet players. Oh my goodness.

Reed. Now you talk about Reed. Two guys. Really good Reed. They wind up to those two guys, man, they had the Excelsa band, the Onwards band. They wouldn't use nobody but he and Kimball on trumpet. They didn't use no three or four trumpets. They're seeing Andrew. They only used two trumpets and ten or twelve piece brass band. That would be alright, wouldn't it? It would be alright, but they had two strong men there, you know. Yeah.
Each man hold his own. Sometimes it's better that way, if you have two good men rather than three bad ones.
No, well them guys.
They play a nice harmony and everything.

Well you'll find that on Carnival Day, like Labor Day when they got all them bands out. You'll have to come out there with a horn and don't know what you're doing. You just got a horn holding up your mouth.
Mm-hmm.

Them days passing. Yeah, he used to take guys out, we go to play a job and he said we'd be shot on the mountain. We'd have a guy with a guitar and he used to be sitting up there and we'd be doing nothing like motioning. Yeah. You know, people got wise to that. You know what a potato man is?
Did you ever hear of a potato man?
No, I didn't.
You'd have to take a potato and stuff it down the horn and make sure he doesn't play anything. Did you ever hear of that?
No.
Ah, that's okay. Come on in if you want to.
Well I know I was coming up.
Okay, you coming up Canal Street? I was coming up Canal Street, was playing a parade and I couldn't get no mellophone.
I was playing an alto, you know, upright alto.

Yeah. The mellophone is round like a, what you call them horns. That's what you call them. We'd call them peck horns, you know. And the Jews have rented all the horns out. I got to have me a horn. I looked up and they see the trombone. I said, give me the trombone. I got the trombone. I said, I'll play peck horn on the trombone. I'll play peck horn on the trombone. I was coming to Canal Street, I was being worried. There's a front, you know. I was, I hit the lick. Ain't nothing come out there.
So we got right to Canal and Exchange Alley.
You know where Exchange Alley is. It's still here. It's still here? Yeah. I asked about that, something about it. She said, you know nothing about it.
Martin's in the alley.

Yes sir. I got there, you know. White folk come right side me, you know. Put his ears to the hall, you know. I didn't know he had something down in his head, you know. Soon I got right there at that alley, whoop. He sure half a brick. He was trying to trouble. He run to the crowd.
He broke his lips, teeth and everything. He just threw it up in the hall, you know. Oh yeah. He'll knock it off, you know.

He's come home. The whole bastard, instead of playing, they laughing at me. I got out of the way to fight, man. He's trying to get that guy through that whole brick in the hall. I want to get all them. We had some awful times though.
Did you ever play in parades much?
This was in the parade.
Oh yeah, but I mean, what is it? Oh yeah, oh yeah.
I played drums. I played drums most of the time. Which one? I played bass drum. Yeah, I played good bass drum. I played it lately so I can't walk no more in a parade. I played bass drum.
You still play bass drum once in a while in a parade out in Los Angeles. What about cymbals?
Cymbals too. How did you work that then in those two? The cymbals and the bass drum? I used the cymbals and the bass drum.
I used the same thing, yeah. The cymbals on the top and the while beat them. Same old time.
Same thing. After beats usually? Oh yeah. On the cymbals?
Yeah, and some pieces, yeah.
After beat, would you come down on the after beat on the cymbals? Oh yeah. On the beat?
No, I'll come on the beat and sometimes after beat. Both ways. Both ways. Both ways. On and after.
What brass bands did you play with then?
Where?
Here?
Here, yeah. Oris Brass Band.
Uh huh. Any others? Did you ever play for the Zaloons?
I rang you when they organized that thing, Padilla and Liberty.
Yeah?

Yeah, I don't know. Kids start that. Little, uh, Sash Moe. Little, little, little, little. Guy, them fellas work out there for W.C. Kyle's a coal yard. Used to drive them dump carts, coal carts, you know? Uh huh. Used to land, let them have a mule, you know? They have a mule. Put in the parade for the Zulus, you know? Uh huh.
And Mr. Janky had a lot of them working for him, didn't he?
Oh yeah. I think he sure did. He used to toast them.
Remember when he toasted them in champagne? Was that during your time? Uh huh. Must have been fun of Zulus.
And then if I, uh, if God died, one of the boys, uh, and the gang would pass. You know these days, they'd start hustling around, collecting, getting the money to have a band.
Oh yeah.

All the second lines that come in, anybody that catch it, put a quarter or fifteen cents, you know? Make up with the one to get a band. And they say band, they'll, they'll sure come up with some change, alright.
Oh yeah. I might give you some change myself. If I can get it. When did the fourth string come in? I wanted to ask you that. Where did you find the fourth string?
On bass?
Yeah.

Well, as far as I know, they always have fourth strings. They always have? Up to mine. But I used to, most of the boys used to take the E string off. Uh huh. Because the finger though, fourth string, most of the, I was playing, I was playing fourth strings, was, I was playing in the theater and the symphony band. Uh huh. Just like Bowen. They bowed. Yeah. And I was in theater. But the man, because of me playing, using the fourth string, Hendrick Kimball. Oh yeah.
You ever met his?
He made me put that string on that bass and he showed me how to finger.
You met his son? Yeah.
I don't know where he was at that time.
Well he wasn't born then. That's right. He was a youngster. Up in the channel.
He was, he wasn't on his way. He was a youngster.
Yeah. Not even a twinkle. Anyway, I, uh, uh, no. Well how did you learn the harmony? You know, to play the right notes and stuff. I learned it from my brother.
Your brother taught you harmony.
Would he teach you with a book, method book or did he just do it? Yeah. Oh you had a method book in it? No sure. How did you learn time? Well a book, what's a book, what you got that book for?
Well I don't know, I had to have a teacher too, myself. Well you had a teacher didn't you? Yeah.
Did he school you at the time? Yeah. Yeah.
He schooled me at time. He taught me how to. 1, 2, 3, 4. He made sure how to move my foot.
You know.
Did you do that? Move your foot in a certain way to keep time when you were taking that.
Yeah. But he didn't show me that. No. And he didn't have no foot work. No. That's why Hoss showed me. You know. It was a time.
It was a time.
For me. For me.
For me.
For me. For me. For me.
For me. For me. For me. For me. For me. For me. making you move, patting my foot a certain way and slide it to the side and all that.
Oh yeah. Counting. Yeah. Four beats. One, two, three, four. Double up. One, two, three, four. One, two, three, four.
What about quadrilles and mazurkas and things like that? How do you count them?
You don't know nothing about quadrilles.
I'm going to hear one Friday night.
Oh yeah?
Yeah, they're going to have one at the festival.
They still have quadrilles.
Playing charters and quadrilles?
Yeah.
This is an antique town.
Didn't you know that?
I'll have to play a quadrilles in the charters.
Well, I tell you. You want to go to rehearsal?
When?
I don't know. I'll call the ladies if you want to when we're finished. All right. The ladies run those kind of dances, you know.
Oh, they run the quadrilles dance. Yeah, that's what I mean. Yeah, well, they're the same as the old timers running a reel. Yeah, they have a-
Yeah, they have a-
Call the figures, you know. Yeah. But here, we have three figures of the old quadrilles. First, second, third, and the fourth. What do you call it?
The fourth figure is fair.

I mean, swing your partner. Oh. Make me get out there and want to do a little dancing. You know anything about Bachaca? Who? Bachaca. That's what you call it when they swing out. Swing? That's what they call it in Creole.
Bachaca. Bachaca.
I think that's what they say.
I don't speak Creole very well. I see.
I'll hoard that. Yeah.
Do you speak Creole? No.
Yeah.
I'm not from downtown. Battlefield. Were you around the battlefield?
When I was here, I was staying. Not when I left there but my people stayed 25 years ago.
And then, you know, I was in the middle of the time.
Yeah, I'm up from downtown.
Battlefield, huh? Were you around the battlefield?
When I was here, I was staying, not when I left there, but my people stayed. 2538 Cleveland Avenue. You know where that's at?
Oh yeah, Gasket Street.
Cleveland Indurgeon Wall. That's where I lived. But when I left, I was staying at 217 South Villa Street.
That's not far from Chinatown, huh?
That's Gaster Street there. Yeah. I was at Villa and Gaster, the continuation of Cleveland Avenue.

Well, they still have the sign on the building there, I think, saying Gasket Street. Yeah? Yeah, it's a ballroom there. It's about, what, about 1400, 1500 block of Gasket. It's still there. You can see Gasket Street on the side of the building. Hmm. You go to the end of the 1400 block, between 14 and 15, and you look around on the building on the Uptown Lake corner. I think that's Villera and Gasket.
That's Villera and Gasket. That must be where, uh...
There was a ballroom there.

Well, what you call them, is that? There's a ballroom on the corner, and upstairs used to be a little club, nightclub. I was playing up there when I left to go to Chicago. Guidry and Allen. Oh. Guidry and Allen.
Fess has told me about that. Hoss told me about that.
Well, that place was Guidry and Allen. Who was Allen?
That was...
There wasn't old man Allen from across the river.
No, no, no. Depend on the place.
Yeah.
Guidry and Allen. No, not Allen over the river. That had the Pacific Brass Band. You talking about Red Howlin's daddy?
Yeah. Mm-hmm.
No, he live in Algiers.
Oh, what?
That was Tom... That's Tom King's building. You know, Tom King's sheriff around here. Not the sheriff. Yeah, he was the sheriff. He was the sheriff.
No, I didn't know him. That was a little before my time. Professor Mineta used to tell me about all those people and places and all that.
Yeah.
He used to tell me about Dandy Lewis. Do you remember Dandy Lewis? The bass player?
Yeah. He used to play with Frankie Dueson. Oh, yeah.
Eagle Band.
That was a...
What kind of band was that? A real smooth band?
Mm-hmm. That was a hot band.
Hot band?
No, very hot.
How did Frankie Dueson sound? How did Frankie Dueson sound? Would he sound... How would he compare, say, with Roy Palmer or Kid R.A.? Did he sound like Jim Robinson or who?
He played hard, pretty hard. He played like Jim... He played like Jim... He played like Jim Robinson. Yeah?
Hard. That one rocked right in. Yeah.
Do you know Roy Palmer? I never met him.
I used to try to imitate him when I had a trombone. But I couldn't tell him. Because you didn't hear that. Not Roy Palmer. He was too old. Willie Carnish? I knew you didn't know about him.
No, but I knew his young wife.
Hmm.
She used to live on Bertrand Street. No, Bolivar Street, I believe it was. Right around Tulane Avenue. You know where Tulane and Bolivar is? That neighborhood.
What do you mean? Here in the church. What do you mean?
Tulane and Bolivar?
Yeah. That's what you're trying to call it? A block and a half. What do you call him? Bertrand? That's Bolivar. That's Bolivar. Ballivar. Ballivar. Ballivar. Ballivar. Ballivar. Ballivar. Ballivar.
Ballivar. Ballivar. Ballivar. Ballivar.
Ballivar. Ballivar.
Ballivar. Ballivar.
Ballivar. Ballivar.
Ballivar.
Ballivar. Ballivar. Ballivar. Ballivar. Ballivar. Ballivar.
Yeah, I mean, you get him right, you know, tell him that, and he knew that.
Yeah.
Anna. That's of course, Anna, that baller in the grave, yeah. I was with him the other night.
Oh, you saw him, huh?
Oh, yeah.
How's he doing these days? I haven't seen him.
He's doing all right. Look fine.
Is he still playing with Punchy?
He's playing, yeah. We played together there. I played a game. We alternate the other night. I played one set, he played one set.
Mm-hmm.
Last time we played, he was playing mandolin, meaning we used to go around, we're standing around with mandolin, guitar, and bass.
What were you doing?
Playing mandolin, guitar, and bass.
Yeah, but where were you playing at?
Anywhere, we was playing for our own self. Oh, yeah. Having good times.
Oh, yeah. I guess I better get another reel of tape. Find it. Yeah. Because I've heard about those bands, you know. Like that.

You know, Eddie played nice man, good mandolin. Played guitar, banjo. And I heard he was playing bass. And boy, she played nice bass, you see, yeah? You know, last time, the other night I got to hear him. She could play nice bass. He got good bass, too.
Yeah, he does all right for a young man, I guess. Right? Yeah, he's doing a job.
Yeah. Thank you.
Second reel Mr. Garland. So we were talking about a string trio you say?

Yeah. With Eddie? We were talking about Eddie Darcy, yeah. Yeah. We were talking about how we used to run around together playing with the trio, playing mandolin guitar and bass. Nah, he's playing bass violin himself. Playing good bass too.
Well Bro told me he used to play that mandolin around town. What was Bro? Bro, Bro told me he did.
I never know.
Yeah, I guess they had a lot of groups wandering, strolling, is what I'm talking about. Serenading bands.
I know I played mandolin. I never know if Bro would play on. I can't say he did.
Well that might have been after you left, because you left so early. Mm-hmm. He might have been out in the country when you were here.
That's right.
Did they have many serenading groups around? Yeah.
Like birthday parties? Yeah, that's what we used to do all the time, serenading. Always go somebody to do all hours a night, serenading. Sure.
What would you do when people got married? Would they have any music or anything?

So, you know, alright. Baby Dots was playing in St. Louis. He wrote to Baby Dots. And he said for Baby Dots. Now, he didn't get permission from the union. Number six, you see. Baby Dots. Baby Dots. And the next thing, he didn't get permission from the union to report to Baby Dots here in San Francisco. He said, you can't report nobody to have it out of the consultant board. Joe said, well, they ain't got nobody here to play my music. He said, well, you don't know that. He said, well, you come to find out. He said, I want a jazz drummer. Dixie Lanzo.
